questions.question: Which of the following provides the most detailed three-dimensional view of the structure of the living human brain? i. PET ii . angiography iii. EEG iv. MRI / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Sexually Dimorphic Nucleus of the Preoptic Area (SDN-POA)
  • • Location: Preoptic Area of the hypothalamus.
  • • Difference: This nucleus is significantly larger (2-3 times) and contains more
  • neurons in males than in females across many species, including humans (where it is
  • called the INAH-3).
  • • Functional Significance: The SDN-POA is crucial for the expression of male typical
  • sexual behaviour. Its larger size in males is directly organized by prenatal exposure to
  • testosterone (converted to estradiol). Lesions in this area disrupt mounting behaviour
  • in males.

questions.question: Recurrent binge-eating without compensatory behaviour is characteristic of: i. Rumination disorder ii . Binge-eating disorder iii. Pica iv. Bulimia Nervosa / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• The GnRH Pulse Generator
  • • Location: Medial Basal Hypothalamus/Arcuate Nucleus.
  • • Difference: While the structure of the neurons is similar, the pattern of activity is
  • profoundly different. In females, the pulse generator produces a cyclic (surge) release
  • of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), leading to the ovulatory cycle. In
  • males, it produces a steady, tonic release.
  • • Functional Significance: This difference is responsible for the cyclic nature of female
  • reproduction (menstrual/estrous cycle) versus the acyclic, constant fertility in males.
  • This "cycling center" is defeminized in males by prenatal testosterone.

questions.question: What is a reflex arc? Name its main components. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is a reflex arc? Name its main components.
  • A reflex arc is a neural pathway that controls a reflex action. It is an automatic, rapid
  • response to a specific stimulus that bypasses the brain. The main Components are
  • • Sensory Receptor: Detects the stimulus.
  • • Sensory (Afferent) Neuron: Carries information to the CNS.
  • • Integration Centre (Interneuron): Processes the information.
  • • Motor (Efferent) Neuron: Carries the response command away from the CNS.
  • • Effector (Muscle/Gland): Performs the reflexive action.

questions.question: What is the significance of the limbic system in behaviour? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• What is the significance of the limbic system in behaviour?
  • The limbic system is a group of interconnected brain structures crucial for emotion,
  • motivation, learning, and memory. The Significance are
  • • Amygdala: Central to emotional responses, especially fear and aggression.
  • • Hippocampus: Vital for forming new long-term memories (memory consolidation).
  • • Hypothalamus: Regulates motivated behaviors (fighting, fleeing, feeding, mating)
  • via hormonal and autonomic outputs.
  • Together, they link higher cognitive processes with primitive emotional drives, allowing
  • experiences to be emotionally colored and remembered.

questions.question: What is the primary role of cortisol in the stress response? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is the primary role of cortisol in the stress response?
  • Cortisol is the primary glucocorticoid hormone released by the adrenal cortex during
  • stress. The primary role is to mobilize energy and suppress non-essential functions to help the
  • body cope with a stressor.
  • • It increases blood sugar (gluconeogenesis).
  • • It enhances the brain's use of glucose.
  • • It enabling fight-or-flight responses.
  • • It modulates inflammatory and immune responses.

questions.question: Describe the role of acetylcholine. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the role of acetylcholine.
  • Acetylcholine (ACh) is a small-molecule neurotransmitter, a critical neurotransmitter with
  • multiple roles:
  • • At the Neuromuscular Junction: It is the excitatory transmitter that triggers muscle
  • contraction.
  • • In the Brain: It is vital for attention, learning, memory, and arousal. The degeneration
  • of ACh-releasing neurons is a key feature of Alzheimer's disease.
  • • In the Autonomic Nervous System: It is the main transmitter for pre-ganglionic
  • neurons in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, and for post-
  • ganglionic neurons in the parasympathetic division.

questions.solution_html:

  • Growth hormone (GH) plays an important role in brain development and learning. It

  • essential for learning and memory formation. GH also increases the production of insulin-like
  • growth factor-1 (IGF-1), which supports neural growth, cognitive function, and overall brain
  • performance.

questions.question: Explain satiation and satiety centre. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain satiation and satiety centre.
  • These are hypothalamic centres that regulate eating behavior.
  • • Satiety Centre: The Ventromedial Hypothalamus (VMH). When stimulated, it signals
  • "fullness" and stops eating. Damage leads to hyperphagia (overeating).
  • • Satiation Centre (Hunger Centre): The Lateral Hypothalamus (LH). When stimulated,
  • it initiates eating. Damage leads to aphagia (lack of eating). These centers integrate
  • signals like leptin and ghrelin to control food intake.

questions.question: Explain how hormones influence sexual behaviour. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how hormones influence sexual behaviour
  • Hormones play a major role in shaping and regulating sexual behaviour through two
  • main effects – organizational and activational effects. These work together to form the
  • biological basis of sexual motivation and activity.
  • • Organizational Effects (Permanent Brain Structuring) - These are long-lasting
  • effects that occur during early development (prenatal or early postnatal period). They
  • help in “organizing” the brain into a male or female pattern. Testosterone is the key
  • hormone. In males, testosterone is converted into estradiol in the brain, which
  • masculinizes and defeminizes the brain.
  • • Activational Effects (Temporary Activation in Adulthood) - These are short-term
  • and reversible effects that occur after puberty. Hormones activate the neural circuits
  • formed earlier, controlling sexual desire and behaviour. In females: Estrogen and
  • progesterone levels rise around ovulation, increasing sexual receptivity. In males:
  • Testosterone maintains sex drive, erectile function, and sperm production. Removal
  • of testosterone reduces sexual activity, but it can be restored with hormone therapy.
  • • Puberty and Hormonal Regulation - During puberty, a surge in sex hormones
  • activates sexual motivation and secondary sexual characteristics. The hypothalamic–
  • pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis controls hormone release and reproductive function.
  • • Brain Areas and Neurotransmitters - Hormones act on brain regions like the
  • hypothalamus, amygdala, and preoptic area, influencing arousal and partner
  • preference. They interact with dopamine (pleasure), serotonin, and oxytocin (bonding
  • and intimacy).
  • • Psychological and Environmental Influence - While hormones set the biological
  • foundation, sexual behaviour is also shaped by learning, emotions, relationships, and
  • cultural factors.

• Illustrate the structure of synapse in detail and list out the types of synapses.
  • A synapse is a junction with a minute gap that separates two neurons (nerve cells), the
  • basic unit of the nervous system in the brain. Classification Based on Structures - Axo-
  • dendritic Synapses, Axo-somatic Synapses, Axo-axonic Synapses, Dendo-dendritic Synapses.
  • Classification Based on Signal Transduction Methods: Electrical Synapses, Chemical
  • Synapses (Excitatory Chemical Synapses, Inhibitory Chemical Synapses). Structure of
  • synapses - The typical synapse comprises three main elements: the presynaptic neuron, the
  • synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic neuron. Presynaptic Neuron: Synaptic Vesicles, Active
  • Zone, Cytoskeletal Elements. Synaptic Cleft. Postsynaptic Neuron: Functions - Receptor
  • Activation, Ion Flow Regulation:
